title: Fingerprinting Deep Neural Networks for Ownership Protection: An Analytical Approach
one_liner: Instead of guessing where to place fingerprints, math now tells you the exact safe zone—far enough that attackers cannot escape them by tweaking the model, but close enough that innocent independent models do not accidentally trigger them.
lead: When you train a big neural network (a machine-learning model that learns to recognize patterns), the weights inside it are your intellectual property. Thieves can steal the trained weights and sell them as their own. A fingerprint is a secret test: you pick a few hidden trigger images that make your model behave unusually, and an honest model trained from scratch would never respond the same way to those triggers. But how different should the trigger be from normal images? Too similar and thieves who slightly modify your model will still pass. Too different and a model trained independently might accidentally pass the test anyway. This paper solves that riddle analytically: it mathematically defines the safe zone where the trigger must land.

paras: You want to prove a stolen neural network is yours. One approach: pick some special images that your model treats differently than an untrained model would. These are your fingerprints. A naive attempt: make the fingerprints as different as possible from normal images, so they stand out. But this breaks: an attacker can fine-tune your model slightly (adjust a few weights) and the fingerprints stop working. Alternatively, make the fingerprints very similar to normal images to survive fine-tuning. But now the problem swaps: a model trained from scratch by someone else, with no access to yours, might randomly respond to those fingerprints the same way anyway, and you cannot prove the model is yours.

Existing fingerprinting methods dodge this dilemma by guessing. They try a distance and run experiments. Some models keep rejecting fingerprints even when modified; some only pass the test when your original model does. Nobody knows the right distance beforehand.

callout.html: The paper mathematically solves for the exact safe distance from normal images where fingerprints survive attackers tweaking the model and stay unique to your model at the same time.

steps.text: Choose images your model is sure about (predicts with high confidence).
For each anchor, find the smallest perturbation (pixel changes) that makes your model flip its prediction.
Use math to derive the admissible interval: minimum stretch to survive fine-tuning, maximum to stay unique.
Multiply each nudge by a stretch factor in the safe zone to produce the final fingerprint images.
Run fingerprints on a suspect model; if it responds the old way, it is your stolen model.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: Before: pick the stretch factor (how much to scale the minimal nudge) by trial and error. After: compute it analytically using bounds derived from the two constraints: (1) fingerprints survive attackers tweaking the model, and (2) independent models do not accidentally trigger them.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: stretch factor and distance zone
hidden.name: Admissible interval for stretch factor
paras: The stretch factor (called tau or τ) scales the minimal perturbation. A larger stretch makes the fingerprint farther from normal images. The paper discovers that tau must lie in a specific safe zone: an admissible interval between a lower bound and an upper bound. The lower bound ensures that when an attacker fine-tunes the model, the fingerprint still triggers the wrong prediction. The upper bound ensures that a model trained from scratch independently will not accidentally trigger the fingerprint by chance. Together, these two bounds squeeze tau into a corridor.

The paper estimates these bounds using two surrogate model pools: a pirated pool (copies of the real model modified by fine-tuning or knowledge distillation) and an independent pool (models trained from scratch with different seeds and architectures). By testing the fingerprints on these surrogates, the paper figures out which tau values satisfy both properties.

heat.caption: Darker means more stable: fingerprints survive tweaking and independent models do not trigger.

reads.html: The paper finds the right distance to place fingerprints so a stolen model still fails the test after modification, but an honest independent model passes naturally.

The admissible interval for stretch factor τ is defined by lower bound τ_lower (fingerprint survives fine-tuning: uses L-Lipschitz constant of independent models) and upper bound τ_upper (fingerprint avoids false alarms: uses sensitivity of independent models to perturbations).

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the math behind the safe zone
paras: The core insight: survival and uniqueness pull in opposite directions. To make fingerprints survive tweaking, scale the perturbation large (far from normal images), so attackers cannot adjust the model to stop triggering it. To make them unique, scale small (close to normal), so independent models do not randomly trigger them by accident. The stretch factor is the dial. The paper translates these two conflicting demands into precise mathematical bounds.

Surviving tweaking requires a lower bound: if an independently trained model has a certain sensitivity to input changes (captured by a Lipschitz constant, which measures how much the model's output changes when the input changes slightly), then the perturbation must be scaled large enough that even after the attacker's weight adjustments, the perturbed image still flips the prediction. Uniqueness requires an upper bound: the perturbation cannot scale so large that an independent model, which has never seen the fingerprint, randomly outputs the wrong class anyway. The two constraints intersect. The admissible interval is where both hold.

Derive lower bound: survive fine-tuning attacks
Derive upper bound: avoid false positives from independent models
Solve for stretch factor in admissible interval

math.h2: The equation and what it means
math.words: τ_lower < τ ≤ τ_upper, where τ is the stretch factor, τ_lower is the minimum stretch (robustness lower bound), and τ_upper is the maximum stretch (uniqueness upper bound).
symbols: stretch factor (how much to scale the minimal perturbation)
lower bound from robustness: minimum scale to survive fine-tuning attacks
upper bound from uniqueness: maximum scale to avoid independent-model false positives
Lipschitz constant measuring how sensitive independent models are to input changes
minimal perturbation that changes the protected model's prediction

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Anchor image x_a: a dog photo the model is very confident about (95% dog).
Minimal perturbation δ*: pixel changes that flip the prediction (0.2 magnitude).
If τ_lower = 1.5 and τ_upper = 3.5, then τ must be between 1.5 and 3.5.
Choose τ = 2.5 (in the middle of the safe zone).
Fingerprint x* = x_a + 2.5 * δ* (the perturbed image with 0.5 magnitude: 0.2 * 2.5).
Test: protected model sees x* and flips to a different class (survives tweaking: ✓).
Test: independent model sees x* and still predicts dog with high confidence (no false alarm: ✓).

math.note: The admissible interval is the corridor where fingerprints survive tweaking and independent models do not trigger; the stretch factor must land inside it.

items.html: The lower bound τ_lower depends on τ, creating a circular relationship. The paper breaks this by grid-searching over the admissible interval instead of solving it directly.

items.b: Surrogate model pools may not represent all attackers.
items.html: The paper estimates the bounds using surrogate pools (a few fine-tuned and independent models). If a real attacker uses a modification technique not in the surrogates, the bounds might not hold.

To make bounds computable, the paper relaxes the theoretical constraints using quantiles (statistical thresholds) over the surrogate pools. This relaxation trades off tightness for practicality; the true worst-case bounds might be larger.

Test fingerprints on a comprehensive surrogate pool covering multiple attack types (fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, pruning, adversarial training), and re-derive bounds if the model will face a new threat.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small CNN on CIFAR-10. Train it normally and save the weights. Apply AnaFP: pick ten high-confidence images, compute minimal perturbations, derive the admissible interval for τ using surrogate model pools (three fine-tuned copies and three independent models trained from scratch). Select a τ in the safe zone and generate fingerprints. Test fingerprints on: your original model (should flip), a fine-tuned copy (should flip), a pruned copy (should flip), and independent models trained from scratch (should not flip). Measure survival rate (fraction of stolen-model variants where fingerprints still trigger) and false alarm rate (fraction of independent models that pass naturally).
demo.closing: A correct demo shows both metrics green: the fingerprints live in the safe zone, catching thieves without false alarms.
